analysis.title: Tracking U.S. Supply Chain Congestion: GS Supply Chain Congestion Scale, Oct 26th; Index Lower W/W, Bottleneck Scale Unchanged at '2'
key_insights: The GS weekly bottleneck scale stayed at '2' for the week of 10/26/2026. The absolute congestion index fell 8% w/w.
West Coast container ships waiting to dock were unchanged at 1. East Coast backlog fell to 1 from 2.
West Coast Class 1 rail intermodal traffic growth accelerated to +18% YoY from +16% the prior week. BNSF was +14.2% YoY (vs +12.5%) and UNP +22.2% YoY (vs +19.4%).

Rail service metrics were mixed. UNP dwell fell to 19.9 hours from 20.0 and BNSF dwell rose to 22.9 hours from 22.8. BNSF intermodal velocity was -4.3% YoY (vs -6.5%) and UNP was -4.0% YoY (vs -1.9%).
Ocean container rates (China/East Asia to US West Coast) were about $8.12k per FEU, down about 0.5% w/w from about $8.15k and up 382% YoY (vs +470% the prior week).
Chassis street dwell was unchanged w/w at 4.0 days for 20ft and 5.9 days for 40/45ft containers.

September lagged data was mixed. Container weighted average dwell at San Pedro's Bay was about 3.2 days (vs 3.0 in August) and rail container dwell was 7.2 days (vs 6.8), far below the 2022 peak of about 16 days.
Big Three West Coast ports (LA, Long Beach, Oakland) inbound loaded containers rose 23% YoY in September.

Door-to-door China to US shipping took an average of 47 days in October, versus 80+ days at peak congestion. GS assumed unchanged transit times for index updating because the data provider gave limited updates.
Truck transportation employment in September implied the first positive YoY growth in 40 months, while still about 4% below pre-Covid highs. YoY growth averaged -1.2% over the prior nine months.
LMI transportation capacity was 34.4 in September (vs 40.0 in August), a faster contraction. LMI warehousing capacity was 39.3 (down from August) and warehousing utilization was 64.3 (vs 59.6).

GS says that if supply chain pressures keep easing, the index could stay more consistently in '1' territory in 2026. The open question is the effect of tariffs and geopolitical conflicts on freight demand, flow timing and the ability to normalize global trade.

sector_views.rationale: Congestion remains muted and the scale sits near the pre-Covid baseline. GS flags transport subsectors to watch, with tariff and geopolitical effects on freight flows as the open question.

macro_indicators.interpretation: A reading below 50 indicates delivery times were expanding (slower) in September. The report's own glossary text states the 50 threshold in the opposite direction.
Transportation capacity contracted faster than in August (40.0).
Warehouse capacity contracted, with less available capacity than in August.
Utilization expanded faster than in August (59.6).

macro_indicators.indicator: Ocean container shipping rate, China/East Asia to US West Coast
macro_indicators.interpretation: Rates are down about 0.5% w/w but far above year-ago levels.

risk_factors: Tariffs and geopolitical conflicts could change the demand and timing of freight flows and slow normalization of global trade.
LMI transportation and warehousing capacity both contracted in September.
Rail container dwell and San Pedro's Bay container dwell both rose in September.
charts_described: Exhibit 1: GS Weekly Bottleneck Index, Feb 2020 to Oct 2026. The caption says the composite decreased 8% w/w, the scale remained at 2, and levels are well below the peak at 10 and in line with pre-Covid fluidity.
Exhibit 8: West Coast intermodal (UNP and BNSF) growth tracking up about 16% YoY on average in October.
Exhibit 16: Truck transportation employee count, captioned as down about 1% from pre-Covid.
Exhibit 19: Combined scale averaged 124 in September, a bottleneck score of 2 but close to 1 on all metrics combined.
geopolitical: The report asks what impact tariffs and geopolitical conflicts will have on demand and timing of freight flows and on the ability to normalize around global trade.
